lawyer:
Dr. Kamal Hossain, with Mr. Amirul Islam, Mr. Md. Nizamul Huq, Mr. Md. Idrisur Rahman, Ms. Sara Hossain and Mrs. Tanya Amir, Advocates ----- for the Petitioners. 
Mr. Syed Abu Kowsar, Assistant Attorney General with Mr. Md. Shamsul Huda ----- for the Opposite Party.
parties:
Dr. Taslima Nasreen ----- Petitioner
Vs.
The State ----- Opposite Party
full_judgment:
Md. Mozammel Hoque, J: This Rule was issued calling upon the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka, to show cause as to why the complaint case no.1315 of 1994 under Section 295A of the Penal Code pending before the Court of the Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka, should not be quashed and/or the order dated 20.5.95 passed by the Additional chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka and the order dated 11.6.95 passed by the Sessions Judge, Dhaka, should not be set-aside. 

 2. The facts, in Short, are that a complaint petition was lodged on 4.6.94 by the Officer-in-Charge of Motijheel Police Station against the petitioner in the Court of the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka, being Complaint Case No.1315 of 1994 under Section 295A of the Penal Code being authorised by the Government under Section 196 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The petition of complaint contains allegations to the effect that the petitioner gave an interview to a journalist which was published on 9.5.94 in the newspaper The Statement, a daily news paper published from Calcutta and in that interview the petitioner allegedly made certain remarks, deliberately and maliciously, intending to outrage the religious sentiment of the Muslims. The said statement was also published in the Bengali news-paper 'The Bangla Bazar' on 18.5.94. On the aforesaid allegations the instant case was started against the petitioner Dr. Taslima Nasreen. 

 3. It may be mentioned that the petitioner surrendered before the High Court Division 3.8.94 with a prayer for pre-arrest bail. This Court by an order dated 3.8.94 granted pre-arrest bail and directed that she would appear before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka, personally or through her duly appointed lawyer if she so chooses. Subsequently, the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka, allowed the petitioner to remain on bail. The trial Court framed charge on 5.11.94 against the petitioner under Section 295A of the Penal Code in presence of the lawyer appointed by her. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid order dated 5.11.94 framing the charge an application under Section 561 A of the Code of Criminal Procedure was preferred before this Court which was registered as Criminal Miscellaneous Case No.197 of 1995. After hearing the matter, this Court passed a judgment and discharged the Rule holding that a sanction as required under Section 188 of the Code of Criminal Procedure might be obtained before starting trial. After making certain observations the aforesaid Rule was discharged. Thereafter, the Government accorded a sanction by a letter dated 1.4.95 which has been marked as Annexure-F to this application. Against this sanction order dated 1.4.95 the petitioner raised objection and after hearing the both sides upon objection, the Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, who is the trial Judge, passed an order on 20.5.95 rejecting the objection of the petitioner by a detailed judgment which is marked as Annexure-G to this application. Alter rejecting their objection, the Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate fixed 3.6.95 for framing charge. Against this order dated 20.5.95 the petitioner moved a revisional application before the Sessions Judge, Dhaka, who on preliminary hearing, rejected the application for revision of the petitioner by this order dated 11.6.95. 'Then the petitioner challenged the orders of the Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka and the order passed by the Sessions Judge, Dhaka as well as the entire proceeding under Section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure before this Court and a Rule was obtained on 27.6.95 which is the subject matter for disposal before us. 

 4. In the background of the above the main subject matter for challenge before us is Annexure-F which is the letter of sanction issued by the Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of Bangladesh. It may be mentioned that this Court in its judgment dated 10.1.95 passed in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No.197 of 1995 observed that under Section 188 of the Code of Criminal Procedure the Court can take cognizance of an offence without sanction. But it cannot inquire into or try the offence except with the previous sanction of the Government. Further, it was observed that it cannot be said that the allegation made in the petition of complaint do not constitute offence under Section 295A of the Penal Code. Making the above observations the application for quashment was summarily rejected. After this judgment the Government issued this letter of sanction dated 1.4.95 which was placed before the Court. When it was accepted by the Court, the petitioner afresh challenged this letter of sanction dated 1.4.95 which was ultimately rejected by the trial Court as well as by the Sessions Judge, Dhaka. 

 6. Before challenging the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner, Mr. Syed Abu Kowser, the learned Assistant Attorney General, has challenged the maintainability of the present application. He submits that already an application was moved before this Court under Section 561 A of the Code of Criminal Procedure in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No.197 of 1995 which was summarily rejected by this Court. The instant application under Section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure is actually a repeatation of the earlier quashing application and as such the present application under Section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure cannot be maintained. It is difficult to accept the above contention of Mr. Kowser in view of the fact that in earlier application under Section 551A of the Code of Criminal Procedure the framing of the charge without the sanction order was challenged. But in the instant application the two impugned order of the learned Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate and the learned Sessions Judge along with the proceeding as a whole have been challenged. So cause of action of the earlier application before this Court is quite different from the cause of action of the instant application and as such this objection as regards maintainability cannot be sustained. 

 7. The learned Assistant Attorney General further challenged this petition submitting that the petitioner is a fugitive from law and as such she is not entitled to move an application before this Court seeking any relief inasmuch as she is not surrendering before this Court. In support of his contention he has referred to the cases of Chand Shah Vs. The Crown, 8 DLR (F.C.), 24 and Khalilur Rahman Vs.The State, 33 DLR 12. It is established principle that a fugitive from law is not entitled to seek relief in the Court of Law. The learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the present petitioner cannot be called a fugitive inasmuch as she surrendered before this Court and got an anticipatory bail and thereafter she surrendered before the Court of the learned Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka through her lawyer and obtained an order of bail there. The learned Advocate further submits that as per direction of the High Court Division she was and is being represented by her lea Advocate both in the Court below as well as before this Court and when she left this country for her personal reason, the Government allowed her to leave this country. In such a situation it cannot be said that the petitioner Taslima Nasreen is a fugitive from law. We find substance in the above contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner. Since she was granted bail by this Court as well as by the Court of the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka and since she left the country within the knowledge of the Government and the Government did not stop her from leaving this country, we are of the view that in the special circumstances of the case it cannot be said at this stage that the petitioner is a fugitive from law. So this objection has no substance. 

 9. In support of his con the learned Advocate for the petitioner has referred to the case of Gakul Chand Dwarrades Morarka Vs. The King, AIR 1948(P.C.), 82. It was observed by their Lordships of the Privy Council that facts in respect of which sanction was given should either be refereed to a face of sanction or it must be proved by sanction or it must be proved before extraneous evidence that they were place before the sanctioning authority. Dr. Kamal Hussain has referred to a case on this point of sanction as reported in the case of M.K. Gopalang Vs. The State of Madhya Prodesh, AIR 1954 (S.C.), 362. Their Lordships in that case held that the lacuna, if any, in the sanction of the kind contemplated by the decision in AIR 1948 P.C. 82 can be remedied in course of the trial by specific evidence in that behalf. 

 10. Mr. Kowser submits that the letter of sanction is self-explanatory and it contained the satisfaction of the Government as well as other requirements. If there is some shortage of any materials to be described therein, it may be remedied by adducing subsequent evidence during trial relying on the decision of the Indian Supreme Court. Let us now consider the impugned sanction itself. It appears that in the subject there is clear description of CR. case No.1315 of 1994 pending before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate Dhaka and sanction was required under Section 188 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Further, it refers to a Memo. No. 338-Misc. 48/94(Law) dated 4.6.94. It has been described that a criminal case has been started against the petitioner Taslima Nasreen in the aforesaid Court, the Government being satisfied fully accorded sanction as required under Section 188 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for proceeding with the aforesaid criminal case instituted against the petitioner Taslima Nasreen. From the contents of the letter it appears to us that the requirement necessary in letter of sanction as required under Section 188 of the Code of Criminal Procedure has been fulfilled and full satisfaction of the Government on considering the materials available is there and as such we do not fine any defect in the letter of sanction as contained in Annexure-F of this application. So, the first submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner has no substance. 

 12. Dr. Kamal Hussain has referred to the cases of Md. Khair Ahmed Vs. Bangladesh 40 DLR, 353 and in. Md. Saleh Ahmed Khan Vs. Government of Bangladesh 41 DLR. 210. Relying on the aforesaid two decisions he submits that lacking of this constitutional provision and Rules of Business in the instant sanction letter has rendered the entire sanction nugatory and ineffective. Section 188 of the Code of Criminal Procedure requires that in order to inquire into the charge in a case like this sanction of the Government is necessary. It appears that the Ministry of Home Affairs has issued this letter dated 1.4.95 to the Public Prosecutor of Dhaka, Mr. Abdur Razzak Khan who made an entry of this letter being Diary No. 433 dated 2.4.95 and the Public Prosecutor placed it before the Court on 2.4.95 and the learned Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate. Dhaka, made an endorsement saying "Seen. Let it be placed on the date fixed on 2.4.95." It appears that this is a letter of sanction of the Government issued to the Public Prosecutor who placed it before the Court. In the decisions cited in the 40 DLR and 41 DLR as stated above it appears that some specific orders of the Government effecting some tight to a person were issued and these orders were not issued and signed in accordance with the provisions of Constitution as well as Rules of Business and as such chose orders were struck down by the Court. 

 13. But in the instant case the order is not like that. Rather it is simply a desire or an approval of the Government to proceed with the aforesaid criminal case against the petitioner Taslima Nasreen and it was addressed to the Public Prosecutor who placed it before the Court. This letter was issued vide Memo.No.175-Misc-48/94(Law) dated 1.4.95 from the Ministry of Home Affairs. The satisfaction of the Government and on such satisfaction the desire of the Government to proceed with the criminal case was just communicated to the Court through the Public Prosecutor and as such we do not find that a sanction letter like this as given under the provision of Section 188 of the Code of Criminal Procedure has not violated any provision of the Constitution or the Rules of Business. Facts and circumstances of the two cases of 40 DLR and 41 DLR are quite distinguishable from those of the present and the principle laid down in the above two cases have no application in the present case. So, the submission of Dr. Kamal Hussain has no substance. 

 14. Lastly, Dr. Kamal Hussain submits that this according of sanction is the function of the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs and not the function of the Ministry of Home Affairs as per Rules of Business of the Government. Dr. Kamal Hussain has referred to a schedule showing the functions of the Ministry of Law and Justice and in item Nos. 23 and 24 it appears that Ministry of Law will function, along with other cases, on the matters of civil procedures and criminal law. From the functions of the Ministry of Home Affairs it appears that several functions with regard to criminal matters have been allocated to this Ministry. But if we compare the allocated lists of functions of both the Ministry of Affairs and Ministry of Law and Justice, it appears to us that no where it is clearly and specifically laid down that the function to accord sanction in a criminal case will be done by either of the two Ministries. From the impugned sanction letter dated 1.4.95 it appears to us that there is a law cell in the Ministry of Home Affairs and that is why at the very out "set it is written like this 

 So, it cannot be said that this function of according sanction is the specific function of the Ministry of Law and Justice and not of the Ministry of Home Affairs. The learned Assistant Attorney General submits that it is a long drawn convention and practice that such function of according sanction in criminal cases has always been given and accorded by the Ministry of Home Affairs and not by the Ministry of Law and justice. 

 15. He has further drawn our attention to Annexure-A(1) of this application where it shows that the Law Section of the Ministry of Home Affairs had accorded sanction under Section 196 Cr.P.C. for instituting a case under Section 29 of the Penal Code. This is a sanction letter dated 4.6.94 given to the Officer in-Charge of Motijheel Police Station to institute the present case against the petitioner Taslima Nasreen under Section 295A of the Penal Code and this sanction was accorded by the Ministry of Home Affairs under Section 196 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. We find force in the above contentions of the learned Assistant Attorney General. Since there is no specific provision in the Rules of Business giving any power to the Ministry of Law and Justice for according sanction under 'Section 188 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, we are of the view that the instant sanction vide Annexure-F cannot be struck down in as much as it is a long drawn practice, convention and tradition of the Ministry of Home Affairs to give sanction for proceeding with the criminal cases in the Court of law. So, the last submission of Dr. Kamal Hossain falls through. 

 16. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case and the, provisions of law as discussed above particularly, the nature and character of the letter of sanction as contained in the application as Annexure-F, we are of the view that there is no illegality in issuing this letter of sanction by the Law Section of the Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and as such  the Rule issued in the instant case is liable to be discharged. 

 17. In this connection we may make some comments on the judgment passed by the learned Sessions Judge. The learned Sessions Judge. Dhaka, without admitting the revisional application, in preliminary objection, rejected the same. In his order he has raised objection stating that the petitioner is a fugitive. But we have already expressed our mind above as to whether she is fugitive or not. The learned Sessions Judge further stated that whether the vokalatnama given by the petitioner Taslima Nasrin and filed before the learned Sessions Judge was a genuine vokalatnama or not. This question was also put to the learned Advocate for the petitioner here. The learned Advocate submits that before leaving this country she has authorised her lawyers by executing several vokalatnamas for conducting her cases in the Lower Court as well as in, the Supreme, Court. Whether a vokalatnama is genuine or not is the matter for consideration by the learned Advocate who has accepted it. If the learned Advocate accepted a vokalatnama duly executed by his client, we are to accept it as a genuine vokalatnama in view of the fact that the learned Advocate is not only an Advocate of this Court, but also an officer of the Court. So, on the question of signing and filing the vokalatnama the application cannot be struck, down. We observe that such an objection as taken by the learned Sessions Judge should be disapproved.
